Affiliation:: School of Computer Science, University of Oklahoma
Data & Platforms: Daily High Temperature at JFK Airport
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Cognitive-Grounded Evaluation: Using established psychological theories to explain and predict human performance with visualizations. (e.g., Applying the cognitive phenomenon of "subitizing" to explain why visualization users' task accuracy remains high for charts with fewer than six categories but drops significantly when more than six are used).

Addressing Representational Failures: Designing and evaluating new techniques to overcome the limitations of standard visualizations for complex data. (e.g., Creating "Distortion-aware Brushing" to solve the problem of standard brushing tools failing to select accurate clusters in multidimensional projections (MDPs) that suffer from visual distortions like "false neighbors" (FN) and "missing neighbors" (MN)).

Task-Dependent Design: Measuring a visualization's effectiveness based on its performance for specific, distinct user goals rather than as a single, general-purpose tool. (e.g., Comparing aggregated, trellis, and spiral line charts not just on one metric, but across three different tasks: trend identification, prediction, and decision-making (measured via a trust game)).

Empirically Capturing Subjectivity: Developing novel user study methods to systematically measure and analyze subjective human perceptions like "importance" or "trust." (e.g., Introducing a "visual stenography" task where participants' free-form sketches of line charts are analyzed to reveal which visual features (like trends vs. peaks) they implicitly prioritize and preserve when faced with visual noise).
Summary Description: Dr. Ghulam Jilani Quadri specializes in Visualization Perception and Visual Analytics, exploring the interplay between Human-Computer Interaction and Cognitive Psychology. His research empirically investigates human perceptual and cognitive biases when interpreting complex data visualizations, particularly Multidimensional Projections (MDPs) and dense or noisy Line Charts. He examines how users prioritize visual features (e.g., trends, noise, periodicity) and how visualization design influences trust, prediction, and decision-making. He applies cognitive theories, like Subitizing and Dual-System Theory , to ground design heuristics, such as category limits in scatterplots. Key contributions include identifying the "visual interestingness" bias in DR , developing novel study methods like Visual Stenography , and creating new interaction techniques like Distortion-aware Brushing to improve cluster analysis reliability.
